how: Vexcel marks 17 sloped LA roofs that already have solar panels. scripts/validate_installs.py drew our model's choice on each real aerial photo (green = we'd put panels, red = we'd skip; % = share of the best sun). Each photo was then checked by eye for where the real panels are.

excluded.why: house covered by a fumigation tent in the photo
large mostly-flat complex, not a two-sided roof
ground-mounted solar field, not a roof

roofs.note: Panels on the west side. We rate west and east equally (86%) and would use both.
Panels on the west side, a side we choose (86%).
Panels on the south-facing half (100%); the north half we skip (66%) is left empty.
Panels on both the west and east sides; we choose both (86% each).
Panels on the west side, a side we choose (86%).
Panels on the south-west side (96%), the side we choose.
Panels on a side we score 78%, just under our 80% cut-off.
The installer also used the north-facing side, which we score 67% and skip.
L-shaped roof: our two-side split doesn't match its real slopes, so this is our geometry's fault.
Low-slope warehouse with panels on both sides. We assume a 27° slope, which makes the north side look worse (73%) than it is on a nearly flat roof.

takeaways: 6 of 10 real roofs: every panel sits on a side our model picks.

In 3 of the 4 that differ, the installer used a side our rules skip (a 78% side, a 67% north side, and a low-slope warehouse's north side). Our rules are stricter than some installers, so our panel counts lean careful.

Installers keep picking west-facing sides: on 3 houses we rate east and west the same and installers chose west each time, and on #6 they chose the west-north-west side over the east-south-east one. This matches NREL's finding that LA afternoons are sunnier than mornings, which our model (monthly NASA averages) doesn't capture. That's our clearest thing to improve.
